strengths: The paper identifies a practical and well-motivated problem: tree-search policies should adapt to the remaining per-query token budget instead of treating that budget only as a stopping condition.

BG-MCTS offers an intuitive, moderately original combination of budget-annealed exploration, a depth-based completion bias, and a virtual-child mechanism for budget-guided widening. The wide-to-deep behavior is clearly explained.

The evaluation covers two generators, two mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, three budgets, and several parallel, sequential, and tree-search baselines. Main-table results are generally favorable: BG-MCTS beats standard MCTS in all reported settings and is best or competitive overall.

The depth, width, answer-reach, node-precision, and qualitative tree analyses provide useful evidence that BG-MCTS changes search behavior in the intended direction rather than merely changing final accuracy.
The paper is generally readable and candidly discusses limited reward-model discrimination and reduced answer coverage. The work presents no major unresolved ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: the claimed fixed-budget protocol is not actually guaranteed. Algorithm 1 begins an expansion whenever C_used < B and adds its full token cost afterward, while the text says termination occurs at C_used >= B. An expansion can therefore overshoot B, contradicting the earlier requirement C_used <= B. Without reporting or preventing overshoot for every method, the central equal-budget comparison is uncertain.

Soundness: statistical evidence is inadequate, especially for the small AIME24/25 set. The paper reports averages over only three trials, two for ablations, with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, paired tests, or per-problem analysis. Several apparent gains correspond to roughly one or two AIME questions and may be within stochastic variation.

The ablation evidence contradicts its stated conclusion that the full combination is strongest or crucial. In Table 2, ablated variants outperform full BG-MCTS in all three Llama settings and in Qwen at 30K; full BG-MCTS is best in only two of six columns. This undermines the proposed mechanistic account and suggests substantial interaction or tuning sensitivity.

The algorithm remains underspecified at important edge cases. The generative score uses the mean and variance of existing children but does not define these quantities when no standard child exists, and it is unclear how the dynamically budget-dependent subtree sum in Equations 4–5 is computed efficiently or reconciled with the ordinary W updates in Algorithm 1.

Baseline and hyperparameter fairness is not convincing. Only standard MCTS receives a documented search, performed on one model and benchmark; no validation protocol or sensitivity study is given for the new parameters kappa and lambda. Baselines also mix full- and sequential-generation node definitions, making it difficult to isolate gains due specifically to budget awareness.

The empirical scope is narrow relative to the broad test-time-scaling claims: only mathematical reasoning, two sub-10B models, and one reward model are tested. The paper itself observes that this reward model is nearly binary, so it is unclear whether the method generalizes to calibrated rewards, larger models, other tasks, or budgets outside 10K–30K.

Reproducibility is insufficient for an ICML result: no code or pseudocode detailed enough for faithful reconstruction is supplied, and key generation settings, random seeds, exact checkpoints, context/token limits, stopping behavior, overshoot handling, and complete baseline configurations are missing.

Presentation is mostly clear, but some claims are overstated. BG-MCTS is not strictly best in 11 settings in the ordinary sense because one setting is a tie, and repeated sampling exceeds it for Llama at 30K. Several figures are crowded, and appendix prose contains incorrect figure references and typographical errors.

The impact statement is boilerplate and overlooks the considerable inference and reward-model compute entailed by 10K–30K output-token searches. This is not a decisive ethical flaw, but computational cost and environmental limitations deserve explicit treatment.

strengths: Originality/significance: Conditioning MCTS selection and widening on the remaining token budget is a simple, practically motivated idea. The explicit transition from broad exploration to late-stage completion is a useful perspective for budget-constrained inference.

Soundness: The evaluation includes two open-weight generators, two mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, three nominal budgets, several sampling and tree-search baselines, three trials for the main results, component ablations, and analyses of answer reach, tree depth, and tree width.

The strongest empirical pattern is reasonably consistent: BG-MCTS matches or exceeds standard MCTS in most reported settings, with particularly notable gains for Llama-3.1 on AIME and Qwen-2.5 on MATH500 Level 5.

Presentation: The motivation, algorithmic components, and intended behavior are generally understandable. The tree visualizations and budget-consumption curves help connect the mechanism to observed search behavior.

The paper acknowledges some relevant limitations, including poorly calibrated near-binary reward scores, omission of input and reward-model computation from the budget, and reduced problem coverage in the proposed data-synthesis regime.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed hard budget is not actually enforced by Algorithm 1. Expansion begins whenever C_used < B, after which an unconstrained Delta C is added; C_used can therefore exceed B. This contradicts the stated requirement C_used <= B and makes the effective-budget fairness of the experiments unclear unless generation was truncated to the exact remaining budget, which is not specified.

The evidence is not statistically convincing. AIME24/25 is small, many differences correspond to only a few answers, and the paper reports averages without per-trial values, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or paired significance tests. Examples include Qwen-2.5 at 30K, where BG-MCTS merely ties repeated sampling at 0.183, and several improvements of roughly 0.01–0.03.

The ablation results do not support the strong claim that all three components are crucial or that their combination is strongest. Removing exploitation shaping improves full BG-MCTS in multiple cells, such as Llama at 10K and 30K and Qwen at 30K; other reduced variants also outperform the full method in some settings. No uncertainty is provided for these two-run ablations.

The main comparison is narrower and less consistent than the prose suggests. On Llama MATH500 Level 5, BG-MCTS ties repeated sampling at 10K and loses to it at 30K. On Qwen AIME, it ties strong baselines at 10K and 30K. Thus the broad claim of consistently outperforming baselines is overstated.

Evaluation scope is limited to mathematical reasoning, two closely sized instruction models, one reward model, and only the Level 5 subset of MATH500. There is no evidence for other tasks, verifier qualities, larger models, or genuinely heterogeneous deployment budgets, substantially limiting significance and generality.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper gives prompts and some search hyperparameters but omits essential generation settings such as temperature, top-p, maximum generation length, random seeds, exact model revisions, and hardware. It provides no code or complete implementation specification. The dynamic recomputation of the rho-dependent accumulated value in Equations 4–5 and behavior at the budget boundary are also absent from the pseudocode.

The data-synthesis conclusions are unsupported. Counts of 'correct nodes' include many dependent descendants from the same tree, potentially including continuations after an already answered node. There is no deduplication, diversity measurement, human validation, or downstream training experiment, so these counts do not establish a large, diverse, high-quality synthesized dataset.

The cost metric counts only generator output tokens and ignores prompt/context tokens, reward-model inference, and the increasing context length of deep nodes. Consequently, equal reported budgets need not imply equal latency, FLOPs, or monetary cost, weakening the deployment-efficiency motivation.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the method combines linear annealing, an absolute-depth reward bonus, and a heuristic variance-based widening score. These choices lack theoretical justification and are evaluated only with fixed kappa=lambda=1, without sensitivity analysis or comparison to simpler scheduled-width/depth controls.

Presentation contains overclaims and inconsistencies. For example, Section 6 is announced as discussing limitations but mainly promotes applications, and the generic impact statement says no consequences merit discussion despite the paper's emphasis on large-scale inference and data synthesis. Ethical risks are not severe, but compute/environmental costs, verifier bias, and propagation of incorrect synthetic reasoning deserve treatment.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a practical mismatch between fixed inference budgets and budget-agnostic tree search, then proposes an intuitive wide-to-deep policy by conditioning PUCT exploration, completion bias, and dynamic widening on the remaining-token ratio. The idea is simple but useful for resource-constrained test-time scaling.

Soundness: The main comparison is reasonably broad within the chosen setting: two open-weight generators, MATH500 Level 5 and AIME24/25, three budgets, multiple parallel, sequential, and tree-search baselines, and repeated trials. BG-MCTS is best or tied-best in most reported settings and is consistently competitive with the strongest sampling baselines.

The behavioral analyses support the intended mechanism rather than reporting accuracy alone: answer-reach curves, tree depth/width trajectories, node-level precision, and qualitative trees generally show early widening followed by late deepening and completion.

Presentation/reproducibility: The method is clearly motivated, equations and pseudocode expose the main algorithmic choices, and the appendix provides prompts, answer-extraction rules, baseline tuning information, and the special treatment of LiteSearch's early stopping.

The paper acknowledges meaningful limitations, including sparse or nearly binary reward-model scores, lower problem coverage in the single-solution data-synthesis setting, and the omission of input-token and reward-model costs from its budget definition. No major research-ethics concern is apparent for these mathematical-reasoning experiments.
weaknesses: The statistical evidence is underdeveloped. Main results report averages over only three trials and ablations over two, without standard deviations, confidence intervals, paired tests, or per-problem uncertainty. This is especially important on the small AIME24/25 evaluation, where several gains are only one or a few problems and many entries are ties.

The ablation interpretation is overstated. Full BG-MCTS is not consistently the strongest configuration: for example, disabling exploit shaping gives higher Llama accuracy at 10K and 30K, and also slightly higher Qwen accuracy at 30K. Some one-component configurations also exceed the full method at particular budgets. Thus Table 2 does not establish that every component is necessary or that their combination is uniformly complementary; sensitivity analysis for κ and λ is also absent.

The stated hard-budget constraint is not strictly enforced by Algorithm 1: an expansion begins whenever C_used < B, but its generated-token cost is added only afterward, so the run may overshoot B. The manuscript does not report overshoot magnitudes or explain truncation/reservation, which could affect fairness when node lengths differ across methods.

The cost comparison counts only generator output tokens and excludes input/context tokens, reward-model inference, and repeated scoring. Because BG-MCTS may create and score many nodes with increasingly long histories, equal output-token budgets need not imply equal latency, FLOPs, or monetary cost. This weakens the operational-efficiency claims, although the omission is acknowledged as future work.

External validity is limited to two sub-10B instruction models, one reward model, and mathematical reasoning—specifically MATH500 Level 5 rather than the full benchmark plus the closely related AIME sets. Claims about general tree-search decoding, frontier API models, and data synthesis are therefore promising but not yet convincingly demonstrated.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix: the paper does not provide code or sufficiently consolidate decoding parameters, random seeds, precise sample sizes, hardware, stopping-length settings, and all baseline-specific hyperparameters. Referring to original papers for several settings leaves room for implementation-dependent differences. The impact statement is also boilerplate and could discuss energy cost and the risk of admitting reward-model-selected incorrect traces into synthesized training data.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant problem—allocating a fixed output-token budget during tree-search decoding—and proposes a clear wide-to-deep policy by conditioning selection, depth bias, and widening on the remaining-budget ratio.

The evaluation is broader than many test-time-search studies: it covers three open-weight models, three nominal budgets, two mathematical benchmarks, and an additional physics benchmark. The main table generally shows useful improvements over standard MCTS and sampling baselines, especially for Qwen3-32B.

The manuscript is well organized and visually polished. Equations, algorithmic intuition, budget trajectories, depth/width diagnostics, and qualitative tree visualizations make the proposed behavior easy to understand. The contribution is moderately original: annealing exploration is conceptually simple, but combining it with a completion bias and an explicit budget-conditioned generative child provides a coherent adaptation of MCTS to fixed-budget LLM decoding.

The authors honestly discuss PRM score saturation, restricted domain coverage, omitted input/evaluator costs, and the method's coverage-quality trade-off. No major human-subject, privacy, or other direct ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully support the claimed contribution of all three components. In Table 2, removing completion shaping while retaining exploration and widening annealing gives 0.433/0.425/0.485 versus 0.393/0.465/0.443 for full BG-MCTS on Llama, and is slightly better when averaged over all six reported cells. Thus the assertion that full BG-MCTS performs best overall and that each component contributes complementarily is not established.

The fixed-budget comparison controls only proposal-model output tokens, not total inference compute. Generative PRM judgments and, especially, five full rollouts per expanded physics node can dominate cost; methods that expand different numbers or types of nodes may therefore consume substantially different actual compute. This limits the deployment and efficiency claims even though the paper acknowledges the omission as future work.

The UGPhysics experiment uses the reference answer during search: a partial node is rewarded by how often its rollouts match the benchmark answer. This is oracle label access rather than a deployable verifier and substantially weakens the claimed evidence of generalization beyond mathematics. It should be framed strictly as an oracle-controlled diagnostic or replaced with a reference-free evaluator.

Uncertainty is inadequately reported. Main results are means over three trials without standard deviations, confidence intervals, paired tests, or per-item comparisons; ablations use only two trials and several appendix studies only one. This is especially problematic for the 60-question AIME24/25 set and for small differences such as 0.176 versus 0.167. Some headline wording is also too strong: BG-MCTS is not best in every setting, for example Llama/MATH at 30K and Qwen2.5/UGPhysics at 10K.

The stated budget constraint is underspecified at the boundary. Algorithm 1 expands while Cused < B and adds the entire expansion cost afterward, so it can overshoot B, contradicting Cused ≤ B. The manuscript does not explain reservation, truncation, or handling of an expansion whose remaining token allowance is smaller than its requested generation length.

Reproducibility is insufficient for reliably rebuilding the results: there is no code or configuration release, and important details such as decoding temperature/top-p, maximum generation lengths, random seeds, hardware/software versions, tie handling, exact baseline configurations, Qwen3 prompting, and implementation of the dynamically recomputed corrected value are absent or deferred to original papers.

The method remains a collection of heuristic schedules with no theoretical or controlled empirical comparison against simpler budget schedules, such as fixed time-dependent depth penalties, staged breadth/depth search, or tuned progressive widening. Consequently it is unclear which specific MCTS formulation is essential and how broadly the gains transfer beyond the selected verifier and reasoning tasks.

The impact statement is boilerplate and overlooks the substantial computational and environmental costs implied by tens of thousands of proposal tokens plus generative verification or rollout evaluation. This is not a blocking ethical issue, but it deserves concrete treatment.

strengths: The paper targets a practical and relevant problem: adapting tree-search behavior to a specified output-token budget rather than treating that budget only as a stopping condition. The proposed exploration annealing, depth shaping, and virtual widening action are simple enough to integrate into existing MCTS decoders.

The main evaluation is reasonably broad, covering three open-weight models, three budgets, two mathematical benchmarks, several search and sampling baselines, and an additional physics experiment. BG-MCTS is usually best or competitive across these settings, so there is evidence that budget conditioning is useful.

The manuscript is clearly organized and generally easy to follow. Its depth/width trajectories, answer-reach analysis, ablations, hyperparameter sweep, and qualitative trees help characterize the induced wide-to-deep behavior.

The authors disclose relevant limitations, including severe GenPRM score saturation, reduced answer coverage, and the omission of evaluator and input-token costs from the budget. weaknesses: The central fixed-budget framing accounts only for tokens generated during tree expansion. Reward-model inference is excluded, and the physics experiment performs five additional LLM rollouts for every nonterminal node without charging their tokens. It also uses reference-answer correctness inside the search. Consequently, the physics results rely on substantial unreported, gold-dependent test-time computation and do not substantiate the claimed deployment motivation.

The evidence lacks uncertainty quantification. Main results report means over three trials but no standard deviations, confidence intervals, paired tests, or per-problem comparisons. This is important for AIME24/25 and the 120-question physics subset, where many reported advantages are only one to three percentage points. Several appendix comparisons use a single run, and the ablation uses only two.

The ablation evidence does not convincingly establish that all three components are complementary. For example, removing exploitation shaping yields higher Llama accuracy at 10K and 30K, while removing widening annealing is higher at 10K and 20K. Without uncertainty estimates, the assertion that removing any component generally hurts is stronger than the table supports.

The algorithm is underspecified and internally inconsistent in consequential details. The formal setup requires Cused <= B, but Algorithm 1 expands while Cused < B and the experimental text terminates once Cused >= B, without explaining how the final expansion is truncated or whether budgets are exceeded. Moreover, the pseudocode backpropagates only raw Q values although selection uses a budget- and running-depth-dependent corrected sum. The purported completion bonus is applied to incomplete deep nodes and explicitly set to zero for completed nodes, making its interpretation as completion pressure questionable.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess. Methods use different generation units, baseline MCTS is tuned only on one model/dataset/budget, the beam baseline is a single unreported tuning choice, and LiteSearch is modified. Evaluator computation and wall-clock cost are not matched. The comparison to standard sequential-node MCTS remains informative, but broader superiority claims are not yet secure.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the appendices. The paper omits decoding temperature and sampling parameters, random seeds, exact checkpoints and software versions, per-expansion token limits, overshoot handling, tie-breaking, detailed GenPRM score extraction, and complete prompts for Qwen3 and physics. No code or sufficiently detailed implementation specification is provided.

Originality and significance are moderate rather than high: the method combines intuitive linear budget annealing, a heuristic depth reward, and a widening action. Evaluation is restricted largely to mathematical reasoning, with only MATH500 Level 5 used, while the data-synthesis benefits are speculative because no downstream model is trained. The boilerplate impact statement also overlooks the increased inference cost and the unrealistic use of test references in physics evaluation. Overall, the promising empirical pattern merits further work, but the evidential and reproducibility gaps currently outweigh the contribution.

strengths: Soundness: The central empirical trend is broad and fairly consistent across three open-weight LLMs, three token budgets, two mathematical benchmarks, and an additional physics benchmark. BG-MCTS usually improves over standard MCTS and is competitive with or better than repeated sampling.

Soundness: The paper includes useful behavioral evidence—accuracy trajectories, answer-reach rates, tree depth/width statistics, qualitative trees, early-stopping comparisons, and component ablations—that generally supports the claimed wide-to-deep search behavior.

Originality: Conditioning both PUCT exploration and dynamic widening on remaining budget is a simple but novel and practically motivated modification of tree-search decoding. The virtual generative child provides a clean way to make widening an explicit search action.

Significance: Fixed per-query budgets are realistic in deployed inference systems, and improving allocation without retraining the base model is potentially useful. The gains are especially convincing for Qwen3-32B and at larger budgets.

Presentation: The motivation, equations, algorithm, and experimental protocol are clearly organized. Figures and tables are legible, and the appendices provide prompts, answer extraction rules, baseline tuning, budget accounting, sensitivity results, and additional analyses.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript appropriately acknowledges PRM score saturation, restricted task coverage, and the omission of input-token and evaluator costs. No material ethical concern is apparent for the proposed decoding method.
weaknesses: Soundness: Statistical uncertainty is not reported. Main results average only three trials, ablations use two, and several appendix comparisons use one; there are no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is consequential on AIME24/25 and UGPhysics, where samples are small and many claimed improvements are only a few percentage points.

Soundness: Table 2 does not convincingly support the claim that every component is complementary or that full BG-MCTS performs best overall. The variant without exploitation shaping (Eq. 5) has a slightly higher aggregate score across the displayed settings and beats the full method in several cells, so the completion-bias contribution remains uncertain.

Soundness/reproducibility: The fixed-budget implementation is underspecified. Algorithm 1 begins an expansion whenever C_used < B and updates cost afterward, which can overshoot B unless generation is truncated; the paper simultaneously states C_used ≤ B and termination at C_used ≥ B. It also does not clearly explain how the budget-dependent corrected values in Eq. 4 are recomputed from statistics stored by backpropagation.

Evaluation: The physics experiments use five reference-answer-based rollouts to evaluate every nonterminal node. The accounting and plots do not clearly state whether these rollout tokens are included in the nominal 10K–30K budget. If excluded, methods may incur substantially different unreported evaluator compute, weakening the fixed-cost comparison and deployment relevance.

Evaluation scope: Evidence is concentrated on structured math and physics problems with automatically checkable answers. The physics set is a non-stratified 120-question sample, and no language, coding, planning, or open-ended task is tested. General claims about tree-search decoding should therefore remain narrow.

Baseline fairness is somewhat difficult to interpret because methods use different generation units: several baselines use full-solution nodes while BG-MCTS and standard MCTS use sequential nodes. Although motivated by original implementations, this entangles search policy with node construction; a controlled comparison using matched node units for all major baselines would strengthen attribution.

Reproducibility: Prompts and major hyperparameters are supplied, but the manuscript does not provide code or sufficiently complete execution details such as sampling temperature/top-p, maximum generation lengths, random seeds, exact model checkpoints, software versions, and hardware. Exact replication would therefore require substantial inference.

Limitations/ethics: The impact statement is boilerplate despite the method deliberately increasing inference-time generation. A brief discussion of energy and monetary costs, and of risks from verifier-guided selection amplifying reward-model errors, would be more appropriate.
